gloss: deadly—the late Lat. use of *mortalis*.
the Messiah; Romans v. 19.

not one of the Nine Muses to whom a Greek or Roman poet would have appealed, but the Muse of sacred song, the Heavenly power which inspired Moses on Sinai, and David on Zion, and the other prophets of Israel.
M. does not decide whether the mountain where Moses received the Law should be called “Oreb or Sinai.” The accounts can be harmonised easily: Horeb was the whole range, Sinai its lower part.

more familiar to us in the description “pool,” through John ix. 7, 11. Siloa was outside Jerusalem, in the valley that skirted Mt Moriah, on which stood the Temple, “thy holy oracle,” Psalm xxviii. 2.
Helicon, in Bœotia; sacred to the Muses—whence their title Aonides.

Cf. the similar invocation of the Holy Spirit in *P. R.* I. 8–17: a higher power than the Muse addressed above. “There can be little doubt that Milton believed himself to be, in some real sense, an inspired man” (Masson).
in Genesis i. 2 the Heb. verb rendered “moved” in A.V. means either ‘fluttered,’ as in Deut. xxxii. 11, where it is used of an eagle hovering; or ‘brooded,’ like a bird hatching eggs.
cf. 2 Pet. ii. 4, “if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness.”
*nine*, traditionally a significant number, being a multiple of three. Their fall from Heaven lasted nine days (VI. 871), as did that of the Titans in Hesiod.

an obvious oxymoron. What M. means is—not absolute darkness (‘pitch darkness,’ as we say), for then the “sights of woe” would have been invisible—but the gloom which half conceals and half reveals objects.

lemma: the centre thrice to the utmost pole
gloss: he makes the distance of Hell from the Empyrean = three times the distance of the Earth (“the centre”) from the “utmost pole” of the globe or Universe.
‘adversary’: a name first given to him when he rebelled: his “former name” being thenceforth heard no more (V. 658, 659).
a double allusion—to Isaiah xiv. 12, “how art thou fallen from heaven,” and *Aeneid* II. 274, 275, *quantum mutatus ab illo Hectore*.
a common phrase with our old poets—Spenser, Sylvester and others; taken from the *alto sdegno* of Italian writers (Todd).

important because Satan denies (V. 860–63) that the angels were created by the Almighty: they were, he says, self-begotten by their own “quickening power,” at the time decreed by the course of fate. Fate, not the Almighty, he recognises as superior.
M. makes him use the most offensive word—not “monarchy,” as in 42, where the poet was speaking in his own person.
satisfy = Lat. *sufficere*.
if I am not mistaken, Lat. *ni fallor*.
struck down, routed (Lat. *afflictus*). *powers*, forces.

the former, being the son of Uranus, is meant to represent the Titans—the latter, the Giants. Typhon, or Typhoeus, is commonly described as a hundred-headed serpent-monster, who, trying to seize sovereignty over gods and men, was vanquished by Zeus with a thunderbolt and buried under Ætna.
the Bibles of that time identified the Leviathan with the whale, and M. probably did so; but the Heb. *livyāthān* was used of any huge monster, e.g. the crocodile, Psalm lxxiv. 14.
the north-east promontory of Sicily, now Cape Faro; near Ætna, by whose volcanic action M. implies that it was affected.

lemma: The mind is its own place
gloss: a glance at the teaching of the Stoics (Thyer). For this conception of Hell as not a place, but a mental state, of punishment, see IV. 20–23.
probably the germ of this famous line is Homer, *Od.* XI. 488, where Achilles (in Hades) says that he would rather serve on earth as a poor man’s slave, than reign over all the dead.

apparently not an uncommon phrase for the telescope. Galileo did not invent the telescope, but he developed it: hence it is generally associated with his name. M. saw him (1638–39). The poet would remember that, like himself, Galileo lost his sight (about 1638).

‘shady valley’; about 18 miles from Florence. High up stands a monastery where M. was said to have spent some days. The reference to the fallen leaves is appropriate, the approach to the monastery being through forests of chestnut and beech trees, deciduous species.
the rising of the constellation Orion (at midsummer) and his setting (at the beginning of November) being attended with storms, the name became proverbial of rain and “fierce winds.”

late Greek writers speak of an Egyptian king Busiris, unknown to Homer and Hesiod. Why M. identifies him with the Pharaoh who perished in the Red Sea, no one has ever explained. *Memphian* = Egyptian. *chivalry*, forces.
Moses; see Exod. vi. 20.
alluding to the invasions of Italy and the Roman empire by the Goths (as early as 248 A.D.); the Huns, notably under Attila, defeated at Chalons-sur-Marne, 451; and the Vandals.

Again in VI. 379, 380, he tells us that the original names of the apostate angels were “Cancelled from Heaven and sacred memory.” So he adopts the view that they became the gods of heathenism, oriental and classical, and here, by anticipation, uses those “new names” (365) which later ages assigned to them.

god of the Sun regarded as a destroying power; “the abomination of the children of Ammon,” 1 Kings xi. 7; worshipped with human sacrifices, 2 Kings xxiii. 10. The name, better written ‘Molech,’ means ‘King.’

having been the scene of rites paid to Moloch, it was “defiled” by Josiah (2 Kings xxiii. 10), and made the common refuse-place of Jerusalem. Previously it formed part of the royal gardens. *Gehenna*, hell; the Greek form of Ge Hinnom, ‘valley of Hinnom.’

the supreme male deity of the Phoenician and Canaanitish nations was the Sun-god, Baal. The collective name of all these manifestations of the god was ‘Baalim’ (plural). So ‘Ashtaroth’ (plural) was the collective name of the different manifestations of the Moon-goddess Ashtoreth (sing.).

or Astarte, identical with the Assyrian Istar and Greek Aphrodite, was symbolised in the religion of Phoenicians by the planet Venus or the Moon: in the latter case she was represented as horned like the crescent moon. Sidon was the oldest, and for a time the chief, city of Phoenicia.

according to the legend, Thammuz was slain by a boar in Lebanon; but every year his blood flowed afresh, and he came to life again. The notion of his blood flowing again was due to the reddening of the waters of the river Adonis through the peculiar red mud brought down by spring torrents.

“Behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the Lord; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold,” 1 Sam. v. 4. Dagon, the national god of the Philistines.

the religion of the Egyptians consisted in a pantheistic worship of nature that took animals for its symbols. Thus Osiris, their chief god, was worshipped under the symbol of a sacred bull, Apis. Orus (or Horus), ‘path of the sun,’ was their Sun-god.
Jeroboam, a rebel against Rehoboam (who succeeded Solomon); he “doubled” the sin because he “made two calves of gold,” setting one in Bethel, the other in Dan (1 Kings xii. 20, 28, 29).

strictly, Belial was not the name of any god, but an abstract word meaning ‘that which is without profit’ = worthlessness, wickedness: hence generally found in phrases like ‘son (or man) of Belial.’ M. makes Belial a type of effeminacy and lust.
flushed; the combination of the abstract word, “insolence,” with the literal “wine,” suggests the figure called zeugma.

i.e. Uranus and Ge (or Gaia), whose 12 sons, according to the ordinary mythology, were called Titans. One of them, Cronos (= Saturn in Roman mythology), deposed his eldest brother, and afterwards was himself expelled by his own son Zeus = Jove, whose mother was Rhea.
the seat of the famous oracle of Apollo; on the southern slope of Mt Parnassus. *Dodona*, in Epirus. There was an oracle of Zeus here.
from Leviticus xvi. 8, where the A.V. has “the scapegoat,” while the margin has “Azazel,” which the R.V. adopts. That the word was the title of some evil demon is now generally held.

the “Dorian” is one of the ‘authentic’ modes in music; Plato calls it “the true Hellenic mode,” and “the strain of courage,” in contrast to the effeminate “Lydian” mode. *mood* = mode. *recorders*, flutes.
i.e. the Pygmies, the fabulous little folk whom Homer mentions, *Il.* III. 5. Addison was “afraid” that M. meant a pun on “small infantry.”
the old name of the peninsula of Pallene in Macedonia, where (according to ancient legend) the Giants were born, and where they were vanquished by the Gods.

lemma: fable or romance of Uther’s son
gloss: *fable*; an allusion, suggests Keightley, in particular to Geoffrey of Monmouth, who gives one of our earliest versions (1140) of the Arthurian legend. *romance*, e.g. Malory’s *Morte Darthur*. *Uther’s son*, King Arthur, son of Uther Pendragon.
The lines to which the Licenser for the Press took exception when the MS. of the poem was submitted to him. It was indeed somewhat early after the Civil War and Restoration to speak of “change.”
deprived of, lit. ‘fined with the loss of.’
there are not a few of these jingling phrases in M. Generally he expresses sarcasm or contempt by them.
the first hint of the design against mankind comes from Satan, though Beelzebub afterwards develops it. *fame*, report.
like “Belial,” is not really a proper name, but an abstract word = ‘wealth.’
some interpret *Babel* = Babylon; but why not the Tower of Babel (XII. 43–62)? *the works*, i.e. the Pyramids. *Memphian*, Egyptian.

Peck noted that Milton’s lines read like an account of some Jacobean Masque, describing one of those elaborate structures of stage-architecture designed by Inigo Jones and brought on the scene by means of machinery, to the accompaniment of music.

M. only says that Mammon discovered the gold out of which the fabric was made, and leaves us, I think, to infer from what follows that the architect was Vulcan or Mulciber—in classical mythology the god of fire and all metal-work, and architect of the palaces of the gods.
‘the softener, welder’ (i.e. of metal), from Lat. *mulcere*, ‘to soften.’ Partly a translation of *Iliad* I. 591 et seq., where Hephaestus describes his fall.
‘the home of all the demons.’ The word seems to have been coined by Milton.

“He alludes to those accounts of the single combats between the Saracens (‘Panim chivalry’) and Christians in Spain and Palestine, of which the old romances are full” (Callander). *Soldan*, the Sultan. *career*, a short gallop at high speed.

Pliny placed the dwelling of the Pygmies “beyond the source of the Ganges—even in the edge and skirts of the mountains.” *beyond the Indian mount*; probably he means Imaus, in classical writers the western chain of the Himalayas.

his application of the ecclesiastical word “conclave” to the assembly of evil angels seems sarcastic: that being the term specially applied to “the Meeting or Assembly of the Cardinals for the Election” of the Pope (Blount). *recess*, retirement.
